items.title: Bob Wilber Interview, 1961-05-01
items.q: Coleman Hawkins walks up to the bandstand and picks up the tenor

ctx.x: Kids, it seems amazing now, but I remember a thrilling time going into Kelly's stables and sitting at a front table, right in front of the bandstand. And the band was playing and Coleman Hawkins walks up to the bandstand and picks up the tenor and one of the fellows in the band says, what do you want to play, Hawk? And he says, body, one, two. And he starts playing. And they didn't bother us.
Any other places you remember hearing in those days around New York? I was there off and on all through those years too.

items.title: Bob Wilber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998
items.q: And here Denny and I were sitting there and it’s Coleman Hawkins, one of our idols, playing “Body and Soul.”

ctx.x: Well of course in those days we had 52nd Street, which was this marvelous block between 5th and 6th Avenue, which had, at any given time there was at least four or five different jazz clubs. They’d often change names and management and so forth, but it was great place to hear music. We had Nick’s in the Village where the group of players that associated with Eddie Condon played, Pee Wee Russell, Max Kaminsky, Bobby Hackett, Brad Gowans, the whole so-called Chicago style. There was a lot of live music happening

and of course the big bands were going great, all the major hotels had bands. Tommy Dorsey would be at the Astor, Benny Goodman would be at the Manhattan Room, which hotel was that — Glenn Miller, all the bands. And there was airshots, every evening there was airshots, 15 minutes from here, 15 minutes from Chicago, 15 minutes, it was just in the air you know. So there was plenty of opportunity to hear music.
